The Korean-American hip-hop sibling duo will take the stage at The Vibe Tribe on 12 September, happening at Bae’s Cocktail Club in Chinatown. The late-night event will run from 11 PM to 4 AM, with the pair previewing their upcoming single ahead of its official release on 23 September.

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by Bae’s (@baescocktailclub.sg)

Described as a mukbang anthem for food lovers, 'Yummy 88' celebrates food, indulgence, and good vibes. The single follows Lil Cherry & GOLDBUUDA’s viral 2020 track 'MUKKBANG!'.

Known for blending hip-hop, alternative pop, K-pop, electronic textures, and underground aesthetics, the duo have built a distinct identity through their experimental sound, visual style, and approach to storytelling.

Their Singapore appearance will be part of The Vibe Tribe, a recurring late-night event featuring high-energy DJ sets and guest performances. The night will also double as a birthday celebration for Singaporean hip-hop artist Shigga Shay.

items.body: “When you meet a man who is broken, pick him up and carry him. When you meet a woman who’s broken, put her all into your arms. Cause we don’t know where we come from … we don’t know where we are.” -Laurie Anderson Back in college in the early 80’s, my musical tastes careened wildly between the unchecked rage of Dead Kennedys and Black Flag and the deep melancholy of The Cure and Joy Division. (There was an occasional detour to the land of the Talking Heads.) Then my friends and I discovered Laurie Anderson’s Big Science . And everything changed. I think I was the one that found it and that was only because there was a song called Let X=X, which appealed to my math brain. Our first reaction was bewilderment. “What?? She no longer loves the color of my sweaters??!!? Huh??” But we quickly realized this was something new that we needed to absorb. It showed us that we could respond to all the grotesque absurdity of the world with something other than anger or sadness, that it could be met with surrealism and a sense of humor and that we could retain our humanity. We thought about some of the lyrics. On the title track, there’s a lyric: “I think we should put some mountains here. Otherwise what are the characters going to fall off of?” The song is all about how the oligarchs and huge corporations are reshaping the world to their will. They’re building shopping malls and freeways and new sports centres and drive-in banks. They’re reshaping everything for their own self-aggrandisement to the extent that we’re no more than characters in their play, and they even get to decide how we die. We realized this was the same sentiment that Jello Biafra was expressing in so many Dead Kennedys lyrics, just from an entirely different approach. The music was unlike anything we had ever heard before, full of violins, saxophones, marimbas and organs. And was that a wolf? It was beautiful and then jarring at a moment’s notice. Laurie’s voice could sound quite soothing or, when she uses voice processing, terrifying. A few years later, I discovered jazz, especially free jazz and it became an obsession which has lasted to this day. It eventually led me to The Free Jazz Collective. So when I discovered that Laurie was releasing a live album with a jazz band and an excellent one at that, I was extremely excited. The band is Sexmob, consisting of Steven Bernstein and Briggan Krauss on brass, Kenny Wollesen on drums, Douglas Wieselman on winds and guitar, and Tony Scherr on bass. They have an extensive discography which is well worth checking out. They like covering pop songs, and giving them an avant-garde jazz twist. I especially love Kenny Wolleson who I’ve seen perform many times, frequently in John Zorn projects. The album, called Let X=X (Live), is full of the classics that every Laurie Anderson fan knows note for note and lyric for lyric, From The Air, O Superman, Let X=X, It Tango, Gravity’s Angel, Only An Expert , and on and on. But there’s new music to be found here as well. Church of Panic begins with a commentary on sadness and suicide and then turns on a dime and is funky as hell. There are lovely instrumental pieces like Looking At The Mo on. There’s an extremely funny (and at the same time sad) audience participation moment on Teachers which I won’t spoil. Junior Dad , from Lou Reed’s collaboration with Metallica, features Reed’s vocals with beautiful violin from Laurie. There is quite a bit of sadness on this album at the state of the world and at all of the personal loss so many have suffered lately, but there is also an ember of hope to be found. It’s a hope that humanity might someday soon rediscover its compassion and decency. It’s a sky-blue sky. Let X=X (Live) by Laurie Anderson Email This BlogThis! Share to X Share to Facebook

items.tags: 書籍 intoxicate 2026 August 書籍 # 漫画 書籍 鳥トマト
items.excerpt: 開業医の娘で女子高生の諸星桜はQ州の片田舎に暮らしており、母親から「医学部に行かん娘なんか、産んだ意味ないんよ」と言われ医学部受験を強要されている。本当は医者になんかなりたくない、本を作る仕事がしたいのだが、許されず、このまま望みがかなわぬ人生になるくらいならいっそ死にたい、そんな希死念慮に囚われ悲しみと苦しみのピークを迎えた桜を一台のトラックが跳ね飛ばした。頭を強く打った桜は「私はお母さんの人生の付属物じゃないんだ」「私の人生は毎日自分のために使っていい」と目覚め、一転Q州を出ることと、東大文学部入学を目指しはじめる。人生を賭けた受験バトル。こうなってはおしまいの教訓に溢れた作品だ。

Julian Casablancas is bringing his musical perspective into the art world.

The 2 October opening of The Singapore Masters Show 2026 will see the The Strokes and The Voidz frontman take on the role of Sound Curator for Opera Gallery Singapore’s upcoming exhibition.

Running until 1 November, The Singapore Masters Show 2026 will bring together more than 30 works by leading modern and contemporary artists, including Pablo Picasso, Andy Warhol, Willem de Kooning, Marc Chagall, and Banksy.

Andy Warhol, Pinocchio with Tires, c. 1985-86, polymer paint on canvas, 304.8 x 462.3 cm | 120 x 182

For the exhibition, Casablancas will curate a series of playlists inspired by its four thematic chapters: the Classical Recital Room, Jazz Club, Recording Studio, and The Stage.

Instead of pairing specific songs with individual artworks, the playlists will evoke the wider cultural environments and creative exchanges that have influenced different generations of artists. The exhibition similarly looks beyond the artworks themselves to explore how music, ideas, people, and other artistic disciplines have intersected across generations.

“Art has always existed within a larger cultural landscape, and music is an important part of that landscape,” said Stéphane Le Pelletier, Director of Opera Gallery Singapore. “Julian brings a distinctive perspective to the exhibition, allowing us to explore these connections from another point of view while keeping the artworks at the centre.”

LISA is bringing her story to the big screen.

The BLACKPINK member's upcoming documentary, Always Lalisa, will open in IMAX and cinemas worldwide for a limited theatrical run beginning 12 October, Sony Music Vision announced. The film will later make its global streaming debut exclusively on YouTube Premium.

Directed by Sue Kim, Always Lalisa follows a pivotal year in LISA's life as she steps away from BLACKPINK for a year to pursue her own path. The documentary charts the Thai superstar's experiences launching her solo career, venturing into acting, building her brand, and navigating a personal life beyond the spotlight — all before returning to the group.

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by LLOUD (@wearelloud)

The film arrives during a packed chapter in LISA's career. She made her acting debut in The White Lotus, performed as a solo artist at Coachella, and became the first female K-pop and Thai artist to perform at a FIFA World Cup opening ceremony, where she performed 'Goals' alongside Anitta and Rema.

LISA is also gearing up to release her upcoming EP, PRESS PLAY, on 23 October, with its first single, 'SaWaDika', arriving on 3 September.

Before its worldwide theatrical release, Always Lalisa will make its world premiere at the Toronto International Film Festival.

Tickets for the limited cinema engagement go on sale on 9 September, with cinema listings and further details available via the film's official website.

items.body:
Xiami Music & Arts Festival returned to the shores of Aranya for its fifth edition, bringing together artists from China and around the world for three days of music, art, film, and more.

Held from 28 to 30 August at the coastal cultural and tourism destination in China’s Hebei province, the festival welcomed tens of thousands of attendees under this year’s theme, “Life is not a track, but a _______.”

Leading the international contingent were Swedish rock veterans The Cardigans, who treated festival-goers to a special 90-minute set spanning their three-decade career. The set included fan favourites 'Lovefool', 'Communication', and 'Carnival'.

They were joined by Tortoise, The Horrors, Frente!, Gallant, Hayd, Christian Kuria, Ivoris, and Zella Day, making up nine international acts from Sweden, the United States, the United Kingdom, and Australia.

On the home front, 15 Chinese artists took to the festival, including Lao Lang, Chen Li, and Leah Dou. Together, this year’s programme moved across indie pop, post-rock, alternative rock, R&B, dream pop, and more.

Co-produced by Damai Entertainment and Aranya, and organised by Xiami Music Entertainment, the festival has welcomed 33 international acts to China across its five editions.

Music was only one part of the experience. Xiami Music & Arts Festival has increasingly expanded its programme to encompass theatre, exhibitions, film, and designer toys.

Damai Entertainment's designer-toy brand LUCKY LOOP was among this edition's attractions, showcasing original characters HEY PENNY, ECHOA, and Kooie. Music and cinema also crossed paths at the festival, where the theme song and closing theme from Dear You were performed.

The festival continued to grow its commercial programme as well, partnering with 30 brands for its fifth edition. Across five years, it has worked with 61 brand clients, with 18 returning for additional partnerships.

Sustainability has also formed part of the festival's operations. According to the organisers, Xiami Music & Arts Festival has established 500 waste-sorting stations and collected more than 300,000 plastic bottles over the past five years, while engaging more than 300,000 attendees in its environmental initiatives.

With five editions now under its belt, Xiami Music & Arts Festival continues to position Aranya as a meeting point for Chinese and international music, while steadily building an experience that extends beyond the festival stages.

items.body:
For Regina Song, growing up has meant learning that love is rarely as simple as the stories we tell ourselves about it. On her sophomore album everland, the Singaporean singer-songwriter moves beyond the romantic fantasy that shaped her debut fangirl, documenting instead the complications that arrive when imagined relationships become real ones — intimacy, uncertainty, heartbreak, and the uncomfortable process of learning more about yourself along the way.

Inspired by Alice in Wonderland, everland turns those experiences into its own dreamlike universe. Across 11 tracks, Song preserves pivotal memories from her late teens and early adulthood, pairing her diaristic songwriting with a world of romance, surrealism, and self-discovery. The record follows a period of rapid growth for the artist, whose breakout track 'the cutest pair' topped Spotify's Viral 50 Global playlist and helped take her music to audiences around the world.

Ahead of her highly anticipated headlining set at HOMEGROWN Festival 2026 next weekend, Bandwagon spoke with Song about how her understanding of love has evolved, turning memories into music, living with the pressure of a global breakthrough, and the version of herself she is finally ready to leave behind.

Your debut album fangirl explored the fantasy of loving someone from afar, while everland enters the less predictable reality of being in a relationship. What changed in your understanding of love between the two records?

As someone who is committed and always feels deeply, my understanding of love has changed significantly. I guess it’s much easier to be altruistic about love when you’re young because there are just some things you don’t understand until you’ve gone through them. Looking back, it surprises me how I went from the “simplicity” of figuring out how to express my feelings to the intensity of dealing with the loss of someone close.

I also thought relationships were all about getting to know someone else and learning to accept them. But I have come to realise that it is also about learning about myself and learning how to accept me.

You have described everland as “a wonderland of core memories that seem to live on forever”. How did you decide which memories belonged in this world, and were there any that felt too personal to turn into songs?

These songs were written during pivotal moments of my journey as a late teen and young adult. And when it happens, I don’t really think I get to decide what inspires me. I just write whenever I feel very strongly about something, or when I feel like I need to process something and get it out of my system.

I guess I like to draw a line where I don’t make anything hateful or distasteful, which might get hard to listen to after a while.

The album draws inspiration from Alice in Wonderland, with romance presented as something magical, confusing, and occasionally absurd. How did you balance that world-building with the need to keep the emotions grounded and honest?

I like to write my music with the emotions and concepts in mind. The world-building comes in between or after that process has been done. For example, I like to write the first verse and the chorus and leave space to build the world in the verse and the bridge.

The concept feels like something that needs weaving, which includes changing some words as well after writing it.

Across the record, you write about beginnings, endings, and the uncertainty in between. Which song was the most difficult to finish because you were still processing the experience behind it?

The song that was most difficult to finish was 'The Sweetest Chapter'. I wrote the verse and the chorus a while ago. But I just couldn’t figure out how or what I wanted to write on the other verse and the bridge.

And it just happened that, as I was trying to finish working on the song in time for the album release, I was going through a really tough time personally. Only then did the idea for the bridge flow like water. It took me two years to start and finish this song.

Songs such as 'Kisses by the Shore', 'Mourning Rain', and 'Mars' use vivid images to preserve particular feelings and moments. When you write, do those images usually arrive before the melody, or does the music help you discover them?

It happens both ways all the time. With 'Kisses by the Shore', it was after a first date by the beach, so the image definitely came first. 'Mourning Rain' came to me really fast because I woke up and it was raining, so I played my piano and sang, “On the very last day, there was morning rain.”

But with 'Mars', it was more like I wrote something really cool, and I thought I wanted to name the song 'Mars'. It’s always fun figuring out a cool concept for a song, no matter which order it comes in.

'But What Do You Think?' brings humour and dramatic flair into the album’s Wonderland-inspired universe. How important is wit to your songwriting, especially when you are dealing with heavier emotions?

I think wit is one of the most powerful things to employ while writing emotional music. I think I’ve used humour or sarcasm to cope with many things in my life, and it’s one of my favourite literary devices. And I think a lot of people are the same.

Sometimes things just feel so heavy that I have no choice but to think it’s a joke from the universe or want to trivialise it in a little bit of a twisted way. When I wrote, “I know that it’s such a small thing, but what do you think?”, there was this sense of satisfaction within me, like I had accomplished something.

'But What Do You Think?' is one of my personal favourite songs from the album.

You co-wrote 'Dreamer’s Song' alongside Alicia DC. Could you tell us a bit about that collaborative process?

I saw that Alicia had posted a reel of the chorus of this song on her Instagram and immediately fell in love with it. It happened that she was trying to find another artist to take on her song, and I was very pleasantly surprised to know that.

It was initially named 'In Love Again', but I felt that this was the kind of song where the title isn’t found in the lyrics. As I was rewriting some parts of the lyrics, I kept playing it over and over again, and I thought that the song felt so dreamy — hence the name of the song came to my mind.

I wrote the verse and the pre, and the rest is history. It was such a fun experience, honestly.

everland is built around memories that seem to last forever. As you enter this new chapter, is there a version of yourself — or an idea about love — that you are ready to leave behind?

I think I’ve met a version of myself who chose to be oblivious to my state of self because I was in love. But in recent events, I have been made to face difficult truths, and I think it forced me to re-evaluate what I want for myself first.

So yes, some memories may last forever, but I’ve been stepping into a reality that I’m more content with. So yes, I think I’m ready to leave a version of me from the past behind.

The success of 'the cutest pair' introduced your music to a global audience and brought more than 100 million plays across your catalogue. How did you stop that breakthrough from becoming a blueprint you felt pressured to repeat?

Pressure is something I’m familiar with. I have to live with it every day. But I think I like to see the breakthrough as a motivation to keep going.

As an artist, I will keep evolving, and I will choose to focus on making art that is true to me instead of chasing a moment or feeling. A friend once told me that good art is good art, and it shouldn’t be only defined by numbers. That gave me comfort to just do what feels right to me.

You’ve shared that you are excited to perform publicly following the release of everland. What does it mean to bring this new chapter to a Singapore stage at HOMEGROWN Festival 2026, alongside artists from the community that helped shape your beginnings?

It’s really cool that I get to actually be an artist every day, as a truly homegrown artist. I’m so fortunate to be surrounded by so many talented and hardworking artists that inspire me every day, and of course, to be able to perform with some of them at HOMEGROWN feels so heartening.

Finally, what can fans expect from your HOMEGROWN set, and which part of everland are you most excited to bring to the stage at Paya Lebar Quarter Plaza?

I’m playing a few songs from every era of my journey — fangirl, the gates, and everland — and I’m looking forward to playing 'Dreamer’s Song'!

items.body:
The Manila International Film Festival (MIFF) has unveiled more honorees and films for its third edition in Los Angeles.

Set to run from 3 to 6 September, the festival will bring Philippine and diaspora cinema to Hollywood with screenings, filmmaker Q&As, and industry panels at the TCL Chinese Theatre. The festivities will culminate in a Closing Night Awards Gala at The Beverly Hilton on 6 September.

Among this year's honorees are late Filipino icons Nora Aunor and Pilita Corrales, who will posthumously receive the MIFF Lifetime Achievement Award for their contributions to Philippine arts and culture.

Aunor, a National Artist of the Philippines for Film and Broadcast Arts, and Corrales, the celebrated singer and actress known as "Asia's Queen of Songs," will be represented by actress Janine Gutierrez, who will accept the awards on behalf of their families.

Meanwhile, Forgotten Island writers and directors Joel Crawford and Januel P. Mercado, together with the DreamWorks Animation film's voice cast, will receive the MIFF Trailblazer Award. The recognition celebrates the team's work in bringing Filipino representation, Philippine mythology, and culture to global audiences through a major studio animated film.

Actress BarBara Luna and Priscilla Hunt will also receive Trailblazer Awards.

The Briones family — Jon Jon, Megan, Isa, and Teo Briones — will receive MIFF's inaugural Generations Award, recognising their multi-generational body of work across stage and screen.

As previously announced, Tony and Olivier Award winner Lea Salonga will be presented with the MIFF Icon Award.

The Closing Night Awards Gala will be hosted by Erin Lim Rhodes, Mark Dacascos, and R'Bonney Gabriel. The programme will also feature Ruby Ibarra and Carl Angelo performing 'Salbahe Ako' from the Forgotten Island soundtrack.

Special appearances are expected from Lou Diamond Phillips, Dante Basco, Jericho Rosales, Karylle, Raymond Red, and more.

MIFF has also revealed a second wave of films for its 2026 programme. The additions include the world premieres of Bench: Body of Work, directed by Tom Lowry, and Francis dela Torre's East of Western.

Bench: Body of Work goes behind the scenes of Filipino fashion brand BENCH's return to the runway following an eight-year hiatus, with founder Ben Chan offering an inside look at the brand's new era and cultural impact.

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by @pineapplestudios__

Set around Los Angeles' Historic Filipinotown, East of Western is a contemporary noir-inspired rivalry thriller starring Dante Basco, Darion Basco, and Dionysio Basco.

Five shorts presented in partnership with FilAm Creative are also joining the lineup: Jamie & Lina Write the Greatest Song Ever, directed by Ralph Torrefranca; In the Morning, directed by Serville Poblette; You Could Have Been a Nurse, directed by Meg Mateo; Naughty Maids, directed by San-San Onglatco; and Silim, directed by Alex Cruz.

The newly announced titles join a programme that includes an advance screening of Forgotten Island, as well as 58th, Eddie Romero Remastered: A Century of Filipino Cinema, Kappa-Tiran, Pinay, Quezon, Manila's Finest, and No Room for Love.

MIFF will also celebrate Salonga with a two-film retrospective featuring Sana Maulit Muli and The Vale: Origins.

Two industry programmes will return this edition: Crafting Unforgettable Animation, featuring filmmakers and creatives connected to Forgotten Island, The Simpsons Movie, Float, and Inside Out, and How To Award Season 3.0, a workshop connecting filmmakers with Filipino American industry figures working across publicity, acquisitions, legal, and release strategy.

Festival passes cover screenings and industry panels at the TCL Chinese Theatre from 3 to 5 September. Tickets to the Closing Night Awards Gala on 6 September at The Beverly Hilton are sold separately. Tickets and festival passes are now on sale via the Manila International Film Festival's official website.

A new Girls’ Generation unit has officially arrived. Girls’ Generation-HRS, comprising HYOYEON, YURI, and SOOYOUNG, made their unit debut on 1 September with the digital single Skibidi via SM Entertainment.

The release features two tracks, title track ‘Skibidi’ and B-side ‘Lowkey In Love’.

‘Skibidi’ moves between house and hip-hop, incorporating Arabian-inspired string samples into its production. Lyrically, the track is about carving out your own path, delivered with the trio’s playful confidence.

Meanwhile, ‘Lowkey In Love’ heads in a brighter, retro-inspired direction, bringing together upbeat brass, a groovy rhythm, and a catchy melody.

Fans got their first taste of both tracks before their official release when HYOYEON, YURI, and SOOYOUNG performed them at the 2026 CassCool Festival at Seoul Land in Gwacheon on 22 August.

Girls’ Generation-HRS originated from the Fake Kim Hyoyeon series on HYOYEON’s YouTube channel, Hyo’s Level Up. The series saw the three Girls’ Generation members competing for positions including main vocalist and center, with the project eventually developing into their official unit debut.

items.body:
Coachella 2027 could be bringing some massive names to the desert.

Tame Impala, Dua Lipa, and Fred again.. are reportedly being lined up for the festival, while BTS, SZA, Oasis, and Radiohead are among the acts being considered for major slots.

According to HITS Daily Double, Tame Impala and Dua Lipa are expected to headline the upcoming edition of Coachella, with Fred again.. reportedly taking the festival's special dance music slot at the bottom of the lineup poster.

Tame Impala's return would follow a particularly big run for Kevin Parker's project. The act recently wrapped the North American leg of its Deadbeat tour and, according to HITS, has seen increased mainstream visibility with 'Dracula', featuring JENNIE, and 'Loser'.

The Australian outfit has plenty of history with Coachella, having performed at the festival in 2011, 2013, and 2015 before headlining in 2019.

Dua Lipa, meanwhile, has yet to perform a full solo set at Coachella. She previously appeared as a guest during Martin Garrix's set in 2017. HITS reports that her team has been discussing a potential booking with the festival for some time.

Fred again.. is also no stranger to the desert. The producer previously joined Skrillex and Four Tet for an impromptu headlining set during Coachella's second weekend in 2023, replacing Frank Ocean.

One major question remains: who else could join them?

HITS reports that Coachella organiser Goldenvoice is actively pursuing BTS, who are currently playing a four-night run at Los Angeles' SoFi Stadium.

SZA, Oasis, and Radiohead are also reportedly being considered for prominent placement on the festival lineup, although HITS claims SZA is currently much more likely than Oasis or Radiohead.

Miley, formerly known as Miley Cyrus, was reportedly sought for a headline slot but has turned down the offer.

Coachella 2027 is scheduled to return to the Empire Polo Club in Indio, California, across 9 to 11 April and 16 to 18 April.

items.body: August 14 - 16, 2026, Peitz, Germany Up a creaky set of wooden stairs to the lofts of the 1810 Huettenwerk of the historic Ironworks and Fishery Museum of Peitz, an imposing building full of old heavy tools for the iron foundry and fishing works in the surrounding carp ponds, is an exhibition on Free Jazz in the German Democratic Republic (former East Germany). It’s a traveling show, having accompanied Jazzwerkstatt concerts and festivals over the years. The first time I encountered it, at a Globe Unity Orchestra concert in Potsdam in 2014, it prompted me to dig for all of the Amiga Jazz records that I could find, leading to likely the most complete collection of East German jazz in New Jersey. Every year for the past ten years or so that I’ve been to the festival, I find myself drawn to the exhibition, like a pilgrim to worship. Each station of the exhibit offers a glimpse into this well documented but still mythical past, with a final station showcasing the Peitz Festival. Created in 1973 by two young free-thinking music fans, Uli Blobel and Peter “Jimi” Metag, both from the small East German town of Peitz, the festival drew other like minded youth to hear both East German musicians like Ernst-Ludwig Petrowsky and Conny Bauer as well as West German musicians like Alexander von Schlippenbach and other musicians from the other side of the Iron Curtain such as Barry Guy and Wadada Leo Smith. The names are many and the history can be read in the “Woodstock am Karpfenteich’ books as well as experienced here , and the story is a good one. Lasting until shut down by the government in 1982 and restarted by Blobel in 2011 under much different conditions, the Jazzwerkstatt Peitz festival of 2026 still draws some of those who trekked by train and Trabi to the original, but is also working to draw in a new audience whose connection to the past is being built by heading to upper floors via creaky wooden stairs. Starting in 2024, Marie Blobel, the daughter of Uli Blobel, took over. Some of the changes Marie Blobel made included moving the festival from the center of Peitz to the grounds of the fishing museum amidst the carp ponds and injecting a festive flair into the weekend long event. With a packed schedule of concerts and a two kilometer hike to the Doener restaurant, festival goers are oriented to the wurst stand, the home cooked vegetarian dishes at the beer tent and the biergarten around the corner. Kids have the chance to make their own music with an imaginative looping station and everyone can climb aboard the “Karpfenbummler,” an electric miniature train that will take you in style from the festival to town to the train station. Coming into its own it the new form, Jazzwerkstatt Peitz was awarded the Deutsche Jazzpreis this past year. -- Gebhard Ullman’s Hemisphere 4 PLUS (biergarten stage) The concerts began on Friday evening with the folk-meets-modern-jazz sounds of Trio Ivoire . In the trio's music, Hans Lüdemann ’s piano and electronics and Christian Thomé 's percussion and electronics are met with the organic tones of Aly Keïta ’s balafon, an African instrument described as a “ a gourd-resonated xylophone .” The music is upbeat and highly syncopated and thus quickly had some of the at-capacity audience on their feet swaying to their rhythms. As soon as the set ended, the audience began shuffling off, around the museum and cycler hostel (the Gurkenradweg - yes, the Pickle Bikepath - passes by the festival grounds), to a biergarten, where a stage has been set up under a lush copse of trees. Woodwindist Gebhard Ullman ’s newest formation, Hemisphere 4 PLUS , featuring a mix of his current electric and acoustic groups, began with a chamber-jazz like combination of Anna Viechtl ’s harp and Taiko Saito’s vibraphone. Disrupted by a crash of percussion, the group tumbled into a pulsating groove. Describing the music as “sculptures,” Ullmann led the group through an alluring mix of the delicate (add Silke Lange accordion to the chamber jazz components), hard-hitting (with Eric Schaefer on drums and Oliver Potratz on bass) and other-worldly ( Liz Kosack ’s keyboard and synthesizer). OM (main stage) A short shuffle back to the main stage where OM , the legendary avant-jazz-rock group, were ready to go. The original group members, saxophonist Urs Leimgruber , guitarist Christy Doran and bassist Bobby Burri were joined by drummer’s Gerry Hemingway and Tony Buck who have replaced the late Fredy Studer, as they did on the recent Intakt release Suedpol . After a short freely improvised intro from Leimgruber, a blast of rock energy from Doran gave root to a swirling squall of tones and the music slowly evolved into a groove led by the two percussionists. Moments of electric Miles colored the rich panoply of sound which ranged from deeply experimental to outright rock. An excellent set. Closing out the main stage for the evening was the quartet Selvhenter from Copenhagen. Saxophonist Sonja LaBianca and trombonist Maria Bertel and drummers Anja Jacobsen and Jaleh Negari crafted a dark, throbbing techno-jazz designed to get festival goers on their feet. It was quite late by the time the quartet’s final notes faded, but the show wasn’t over … yet, as drummer Willi Kellers and organizer Wolfgang ‘Assi’ Gloede were hosting a jam session in the cozy workshop building behind the main stage. Amongst painted fish sculptures and some serious looking tools, saxophonist Lotte Anker , keyboardist Liz Kosack and bassist Reza Askari joined Kellers in free-jazz improvisation that began with electronic percolations and slowly crescendoing notes that eventually balled into an exciting and thorny tumbleweed of sound. Following the opener, Gloede curated combinations of professional and hobbyist musicians who improvised into the wee hours. -- Wanja Slavin (sitting far right) (church) Saturday’s full schedule began in the town church where saxophonist and festival Improviser-in-Residence Wanja Slavin , last year’s winner of the Brandenburg Jazzpreis - an award developed by Jazzwerkstatt and the state of Brandenburg - debuted a new composition with a band comprised of Peter Evans on trumpet, Leonard Huhn on bass clarinet, Almut Kühne with vocals and Kaja Draksler on piano. The rich 45-minute piece moved seamlessly between moods and approaches as darker moments were balanced by more hopeful passages. Repetitive arpeggios and prominent electronics formed a consistent tonal base accentuated by the dissonant church organ and several outstanding solos. A short while later back at the festival grounds, percussionist and singer Mariá Portugal’s EROSÃO septet took the stage in the rapidly heating up early afternoon. The music began with a brass fanfare as the group walked-on the stage and transitioned to Portugal singing over polyrhythmic accompaniment. Concentrated on a repertoire of songs that drew heavily on her Brazilian background, Portugal’s vocals took center stage, while the high-powered group of saxophonists Lotte Anker and Angelika Niescier , trombonists Matthias Müller and Moritz Wesp , tubist Carl Ludwig Hübsch and bassist Reza Askari provided solid support. Afterwards in the Huettenwerk building, the duo of Mohammad Mostafa Heydarian and Valentin Portron , performing on the traditional Iranian tanbur and bendir - a stringed instrument and hand drum - continued the expansion of the festival’s musical purview. Impro-Concert: Tony Buck, Matthias Mueller, Taito Saito (workshop) Two improvisation sessions, tucked away in the workshop building, injected a bit of the unexpected into the afternoon. The first introduced the British woodwindist Tamar Osborn with the American bassist Nick Dunston and drummer Gerry Hemingway . This first meeting proved fruitful. Clicking quickly, Osborn leaned into the deeper registers of her baritone sax, while Hemingway contributed a lithe, but full, pulse and Dunston provided a melodically swinging bridge between the two. The later improvisation session joined three Berlin based improvisors who have been in each other’s orbits but never played together before. Vibraphonist Taiko Saito , trombonist Matthias Müller and drummer Tony Buck played a set ranging from contemplative to combustive. Aki Takase, Robert Landfermann, Christian Lillinger. (c) Cristina Marx/Photomusix The mid-afternoon offered both unforgiving sun and an excellent set from pianist Aki Takase who was performing her upbeat, complex, and often humor-laced music with drummer Christian Lillinger and bassist Robert Landfermann on the main stage. The trio’s music is impressive, Lillinger, with his agitated, driving approach is a perfect rhythmic partner for Takase’s own intensity, and Landfermann’s rhythmic and melodic playing adds a nicely fitting layer. Nearing the end of the set, a dramatic moment ensured when Takase suddenly collapsed from the heat. Fortunately, it was reported that the pianist was already on the move to the next concert in Austria that evening. Darius Jones & Otomo Yoshihide Quartet. (c) Cristina Marx/Photomusix A little later the shows were back in the biergarten, where the trees provided some relief from the 100 degree heat, and the Czech quartet Edemit added a jolt of avant-rock to the day while Neiscer and Portugal picked up in a duo form the earlier set. As the day began to cool, the action moved back on the main stage where Darius Jones and Otomo Yoshihide (alto saxophone and guitar, respectively) augmented by bassist Nick Dunston and drummers Gerald Cleaver and Yasuhiro Yoshigaki provided an electric set. Following a rousing Coltrane-like introduction, the rhythm section gave Jones a rumbling foundation for his soaring melody to which Yoshihide responded with a feedback-laden solo, pushing the music to an early peak. The music ebbed and flowed, from dark atmospheric wanderings to high-energy free-jazz explosions over pulsating rhythms. Afterwards, the UK-based Ill Considered featuring Tamar Osborn ( Idris Rahman on saxophone, Liran Donin on bass, Emre Ramazanoglu on drums and Osborn with various woodwinds) closed out the night with a set heavy on beats and Middle Eastern-tinged scales. The set ended with about half the remaining audience dancing in front of the stage. -- Perhaps in normal times, it would have been a disappointment but after the previous day’s oven-like disposition, the cool, rain-soaked grey morning greeting festival goers on Sunday was welcome. A church service in the Huettenwerk started the day for the faithful while out on the festival yard, the others were huddling under the drink stand tents sipping coffee while the bratwurst man started up his grill. First musical act, Richard Koch’s Ray of Light was the only one to be seen under the steadily raining sky. They began with the trumpeter playing a regal anthem and launching into a cheery, melodic tune filled with the folkish sounds of Fabiana Striffler ’s violin and Valentin Butt ’s accordion along with the rhythm support of Andreas Lang ’s bass and Nora Thiele ’s frame drums. The “gute laune” (good mood) music with its blend of up-tempo jazz, classical and folk elements provided a lighthearted start to another long day of music. Their timing was perfect too, as Ray of Light reached the end of their set, the first beams of sun reached the festival grounds. Have You Ever Been Experienced. (c) Cristina Marx/Photomusix The opening set was followed by Brandenburg Jazzpreis. Prize winner, guitarist Andreas Willers , who was to present his Hendrix inspired group Have You Ever Been Experienced , featuring a top-notch group of Berlin based musicians: Amy Green on vocals, Rieko Okuda on piano, Jan Roder on bass and Christian Marien on drums, was unfortunately too ill to attend. Despite this, the group, still gave a rousing performance, taking well-worn Hendrix themes and spinning them anew. Okuda took over the guitar solos with a distorted synthesizer, while Roder and Marien made sure the foundations were securely fortified. Most revelatory were Green’s vocals, which retained enough of the melody for song-recognition and enough improvisational liberty to free them from nostalgic interpretation -- for example, an updated interpretation of Allen Ginsberg’s Howl set to a free-jazz take of ‘If 6 was 9.’ The final two sets of the festival moved back into town to the church. The first was the Polish duo of vocalist Maniucha Bikont and bassist Ksawery Wójciński performing a set of haunting folksongs. Discovered through Bikont’s musicology research, the songs came from a disappearing tribe in the Ukraine, with themes that touched on the universal: suffering, responsibility and expecting better manners from the dead. Performed solely with voice and bass, the music filled the church mesmerizingly. Konradism. (c) Cristina Marx/Photomusix The closing set to the festival may have also been one of the most anticipated. Connecting the festival’s eras, trombonist and archetype of the original Peitz festival and East German free-jazz in general, trombonist Conny Bauer presented the large group Konradisms with an extended composition of “chamber big-band” that mixed generous improvisation and dramatic riffs. Joining Bauer was a cross section of a younger generation of German-based musicians: Nils Wogram on trombone, Maxine Troglauer also on bass trombone, Gerhard Gschlössl on tuba, Claudio Puntin on bass clarinet, Maria Reich on violin, Emily Wittbrodt on cello, Matthias Bauer on bass, Dag Magnus Narvesen on drums and Rieko Okuda on piano. Often breaking into small combos - trombone and piano, tuba and violin - the solos would grow intense and eventually congeal around common themes. A stand out was Puntin whose bass clarinet playing ranged from the sound of a flute to deep, woody resonance. After an intense two and half days of music, the two last concerts were a satisfying and full-circle-moment ending to the festival. Overall, one could sense a tilt towards the new - nights that ended with experimental but danceable music, a series of risky but successful workshop concerts with musicians meeting for the first time, an infusion of world-music elements, and a loosening, but not denying, deference to the past, showing a way forward. More about the Peitz festival: Review of the 50th Anniversary Peitz Festival Review of the Jazzwerkstatt Peitz Boxset Jazzwerkstatt Peitz website . Email This BlogThis! Share to X Share to Facebook

items.body: Label: True Sound Recordings, 2026 Personnel - Jason Kao Hwang: violin; Ken Filiano: bass; Andrew Drury: drums, percussion. American violinist Jason Kao Hwang, a mainstay of New York’s downtown avant-garde scene, reunites with his highly adaptable Human Rites Trio, featuring bassist Ken Filiano and drummer/percussionist Andrew Drury, for a new album. Second Life comprises four extended Hwang compositions delineated by rich ebbing and flowing exchanges and constantly shifting passages, enriched by unconventional melodic constructions and perceptible rhythmic ripples. “ Galaxies Twist Under Before It ” initially unfolds over a 12-beat bass groove that mutates into a 4/4 funk-rock scenario. Hwang’s screaming solo explores several registers of the violin through euphoric improvisational flurries, supported by Drury’s sagacious fills. The drummer has ample space to expand his chops, and the trio reaches a crescendo through deliberate deconstructions. A quieter passage of plucked violin and understated drumming welcomes Filiano’s solo. After the theme returns, the trio enters a reflective state marked by lachrymose violin, tactful arco work, and colorful cymbal splashes. “ What to Keep, What to Let Go ” begins as a ballad, but its gradual expansions and contractions lead into an improvised scenario packed with energy. There are great moments to savor during Hwang’s improvisation, but one cannot overlook the outstanding work of the rhythm section, which introduces radical shifts while toggling between marching postures and swinging delirium. Filiano’s excellent arco technique and deep, resonant sound are are something to be reckoned with. “ Ricochet ” offers motif-inflected tapestries, funk grooves, and avant-chamber passages centered on improvisation. Drury lays down a skillfully articulated and harmonious percussive flow here. Honest expressionism is integral to the trio’s style, with each creative idea pushed into free and open territory. items.body: "There is no such thing as a stranger�s children." - old Ukrainian saying I�ve long been affected, indeed somewhat obsessed, by what�s happening in Ukraine, partly because of one of my favorite bands, DakhaBrakha. I went to Kyiv to see them at the time of the Maidan protests, just after the shooting by snipers of over a hundred protesters. I intentionally didn�t read this album�s booklet notes before listening, so that I could react to it without sympathetic pre-judgement, just as music. It�s strong musically and vocally by any standards, Ukrainian or otherwise. When I did then turn to the notes that translate and explain the songs, I had that rare experience, for me, of becoming moist-eyed. The songs are a mix of traditional and original. They are focused on the abduction by Russia of about 20,000 Ukrainian children who have been taken from their parents in Russian-occupied eastern Ukraine and sent to Russia, in an attempt to turn them into haters of their native land and people. It�s a heinous war crime. Marichka is a Ukrainian-Canadian singer who moves between Canada and her homeland. For this album she�s gathered two groups of musicians, one in each country. Both ensembles contribute vocals and instrumentation, mostly bowed strings, plus some bandura and piano. The group in Ukraine includes Lisa from the destroyed and invaded city of Mariupol, playing a solo on double ocarina; at 16 she was one of the stolen children but managed to return to Ukraine. Daughters of Donbas � co-led by Marichka and singer/bandurist Alina Kuzma, who shares the lead vocal role � is an all-female ensemble in Canada that tours performing these songs. �Foreign Land� is a reworking of a traditional song about the young girls who were sent away to work in foreign households - Marichka�s grandmother was one of these - that can also be taken to refer to the plight of today�s stolen children. The translation goes: A mother packed up her daughter To leave for a strange land To a strange land with strange people Oh, who will pity you, my daughter? Those who will beat me will pity me I'll never again live with you, my mother When, my daughter, should I expect you to come home? When the grass in the garden grows, my mother The grass grew and grew and began to dry The mother was waiting for her daughter to return, and began to cry Did you hear, my mother, how I came to you? How I flew as a bird above your window? How I cooed like a dove? If, my daughter, I could hear you I would open all the doors and windows To let you fly in Songs of Stolen Children by Daughters of Donbas, Alina Kuzma, Zo� Santo As befits the song, Marichka�s vocal here is gentle. But in the second track, �Rusalka,� with Alina Kuzma taking the lead vocals, things turn harsh and fierce. A rusalka is a mythical creature, a nature spirit of fields, forest and rivers, that features in traditional ritual songs. The melody of this one is by Zo� Santo and Kuzma, with lyrics drawing on tradition and the composition of Santo and 19thC Ukrainian poet and folklorist Taras Shevchenko. An ominous double-bass drone, chunking strings, a slithering vocal that moves into sections of white-voice fast recitative and expands into a soaring wild cry. The lyrics are very dark, perhaps evoking the hell of the front line: Home a hell of old growth stumps Marsh a mud of memories Don�t get bogged down in these parts Your kind won�t last a day in here While witches still fly, while roosters have yet to crow, Come here, something arises, �neath the oak something walks. A rusalka sat on a white birch, rusalky asked girls for shirts. Long fingers and nails so sharp Tongue forked round serrated teeth Moss grows down beneath her parts Weeds braided from ear to ear While witches still fly, while roosters have yet to crow, Come here, something arises, �neath the oak something walks. �Girls, my friends, give me your shirts. Though I�m thin, give me a thin one.� Here live us the backless ones Many voices of dead sons You are right to quake in fear Send your sinful children here �Who Am I� is a plea of separation and disorientation, the pain and confusion of an abducted child, contrasting �the human in me� and �the creature in me,� like an internalized riddle-song, with the refrain, in English: Who am I for you? Who am I for me? Do you know me? Really know me? �Enchantress,� passionately sung by Kuzma to her own bandura accompaniment, a girl�s lament of the loss of her brave love taken from her by the enchantress, who is an allegory of war, is based on a traditional song and uses that style of melody and lyrics, �Riddle,� sung by Marichka, reworks a traditional riddle song to be the riddles told by the grandfather of a child, 12-year-old Kira from Mariupol, who experienced the death of her father and her abduction to Russia. Her grandfather tracked her down, and brought her back, traumatized, and asked her riddles - as the notes say �to jog her memory, and remind her who she was, where her home was, and of her family�s love for her.� Songs of Stolen Children by Daughters of Donbas, Marichka �4.5.0� is a military expression for �all�s well� or �all is quiet.� The song is a message, as from a mother, to a stolen child. Marichka�s voice is cherishing: Remember this: I am with you, I am here Don't give up, I'm with you. Don't give up, I'm with you Your hope is my weapon Don't be sad, I'm with you 4.5.0. will be again �breaking into a tearing howl: And when the world's axis breaks When the sky folds like a parchment Out of nowhere her words will come� �and back to fragile reassurance �It's all right, I'm here, I'm here� "Lullaby," based on a traditional lullaby, sung by Alina Kuzma to accompaniment by her bandura and Zo� Santo's viola, starts in gentle lullaby style, but moves to a lament; it's for the stolen children and those who, as the notes put it, 'have been stolen for ever.' Songs of Stolen Children by Daughters of Donbas, Marichka �Remember, I Believe in You� is a powerful piece of harmonizing vocals and slithering strings. Here�s the story it�s based on: Yevhen lived in Mariupol with his three young children. During the siege they lived in a basement bomb shelter for months. One day, Russian soldiers entered their bomb shelter. Yevhen was taken to a filtration camp and separated from his children who were all taken to a hospital and then to Russian summer �camp�. In the filtration camp Yevhen was brutally tortured and forced to sleep standing on one leg. He tried to fall asleep, whispering prayers for his children: �Everything will be fine, I believe in you.� After his release he walked 30 kilometers to the place where his children had been taken but it was too late. They had already been sent to Moscow. Yevhen learned of this after receiving a text from one of his children who had found an unattended device. He traveled thousands of kilometers, crossed the borders of three countries, endured checks, interrogations and danger to reach Moscow and take his children home. All those days he tirelessly repeated to himself, �I believe in myself, I believe in my kids. Everything will be good.� �Another Heaven,� sung by Marichka with the ensemble in Ukraine, is inspired by another heart-rending story: Ilya was 9 years old when his mother was killed by a rocket strike right in front of him. He was taken to a hospital in occupied Donetsk, where 15 pieces of shrapnel were removed from his body without anesthesia. After he appeared in a report on Russian television, Ilya�s grandmother learned his location. She managed to bring her grandson to Kyiv, where he lives now, experiencing missile attacks every night. At age 11, he says that it is up to everyone to fight enemies, to protect other cities, and to build another heaven, where your home will not be destroyed. In 2014, during the Kyiv Maidan protests, Marichka wrote and performed �Red Boots Tango,� using a melody she�d put to a poem by Taras Shevchenko. For this album she sings it again in Ukraine, with the ensemble there adding swirling, classic tango-style strings. Songs of Stolen Children by Daughters of Donbas, BanduraGirl The final track on the album is a solo, recorded in Kyiv, by Anastasiya Voytyuk, accompanying herself on the older, simpler form of bandura that was used by kobzars to accompany epic poetry, and also on the nowadays more well-known big, heavy form developed from it in Soviet times that was made mainly in the piano factory at Chernihiv. Her song, �Soon I Will Be Back,� is based on a poem by novelist, journalist and war crime researcher Victoria Amelia, who was killed in 2023, in the city of Kramatorsk in Donbas, by a Russian rocket. items.body: Palagoma is not only the first release from Nairobi-based label Cool Waters, it also marks the first time German-born, Kenya-based percussionist Sven Kacirek has collaborated with Ogoya Nengo and Olith Ratengo at the same time. Odd Okoddo, the duo of Kacirek and Ratengo, has been performing since 2018, but with the inclusion of the 83 year old Nengo, a singer from the eastern part of the country, there�s an added traditional depth to the music. A 2025 performance shows Nengo�s lifetime of experience singing Kenya�s dodo tradition around 2 and half minutes in (see below). Furthermore, her inclusion on this album allows her and Ratengo to toss the vocals back and forth as they reference their shared roots (Ratengo and Nengo live minutes from each other). Musically, however, the tracks are driven by Kacirek�s Buchla synth, hand percussion, and occasional kit drumming, which serve to buoy the voices without blotting out the music�s origins. Palagoma by Odd Okoddo & Ogoya Nengo �Bara,� for example, begins with the dime-store thwack of a repeated pattern, a stiff juxtaposition to the voices; yet, as the song rolls along, a 4/4 clink appears, then a burbling bass, and finally, what sounds like a xylophone. Layers of synthesized polyrhythms keep presenting themselves with a subtlety almost unnoticeable, until, by the track�s end, it feels organic, as if it�s all been underneath the two voices all along. Palagoma by Odd Okoddo & Ogoya Nengo �Sarah,� perhaps the album�s most intense track, features a lead vocal from Ratengo and tentative, percussive spittles from Kacirek. And while the technology never tries to overtake the vocals, it does sneak up and punctuate the track�s urgency, as edgy distortion sneaks in here and there just as Ratengo�s voice reaches its peak. The term �folktronica� has been bandied about as a way to house the type of music on offer here. In fact, exploratory collaborations such as Chouk Bwa & The �ngstr�mers as well as much of Kampala, Uganda�s Nyege Nyege label house sounds that might be �folktronic� in some way. What�s more interesting and important about this music, though, is how truly global so much of it is while maintaining a deep connection to Africa and its diasporic communities. The music on Palagoma , as well as much of what�s linked above (and available in countless other recent recordings) demonstrates a real willingness for cultures to respond to each other without trampling traditions altogether. Instead, roots become avant-garde and innovations become seemingly thousands of years old. Certainly the inclusion of an 83 year old traditional Kenyan singer only recently making her global debut as she tours with a duo whose instrumental voice is a white male saturated in electronic Kenyan rhythms demonstrates this blurring. The music this trio makes is certainly of the 21st century, but it�s often hazy, sparse, and open, keeping it from a quick sell-by date or confining it to a specific genre. Instead, it�s a beautiful example music as grace.

items.body:
According to its founder, Eugene Rodriguez, who also sings and plays on the record, Los Cenzontles is a �musical group and non-profit organization, which I founded over thirty years ago.�  As he continues in the album�s liner notes, the group �has a long history of producing projects exploring Mexico�s deep roots and our connections with various traditions that, so far, have included Irish, Louisiana Creole, Cuban, American cowboy, classical, pop, rock, and blues�, the latest of which is
Adios Ke Aloha: Waves of the Same Sea
. Los Cenzontles translates to the mockingbird, or, from its Aztec root word, the bird of four hundred voices. This is a fitting name for the range of musical diversity represented here.
With songs sung in Spanish, Hawaiian, and English, the concept traces back to the legacy of Mexican cowboys who travelled from California to the Hawaiian Islands to wrangle the long-horned cattle introduced there in the nineteenth century. They also brought the guitar. The 16 tracks feature old Hawaiian songs with new Spanish lyrics, old Mexican songs with new Hawaiian lyrics, new compositions, and traditional Americana. Yet it is an entirely cohesive musical package held together by dense arrangements of ukuleles, guitars, Mexican harp, and accordion.
Sonny Lim & David Hidalgo
Besides their distinctive voices, the headline artists Taj Mahal and David Hidalgo provide the gravitas and musicianship that their long and distinguished careers have earned. According to the liner notes, they were the catalysts behind the project and facilitated the choice of songs, arrangements, and played a range of instruments. On vocals they are joined by Hawaiian natives Gary Haleamau, Sheldeen Haleamau, Sonny Lim, and long-time Cenzontles member Fabiola Trujillo.
Deportee
To give a taste of the sessions, included before the traditional �Fishin� Blues� is Taj Mahal teaching the musicians how to play it. Sung by David Hildalgo,  the lovely �A Matter of Time� comes from the 1984 album
Will the Wolf Survive
by his most famous project, Los Lobos. Another standout for me, �Navegar� features a slack string guitar solo reminiscent of Duane Eddie and one of many tasty lap steel turns by Sonny Lim. Their interpretation of Woody Guthrie's �Deportee� moves into social commentary, highlighting the cruel realities of being a migrant worker in America.
Vaquero Paniolo
Recorded over five days, mostly live in one room at the Los Cenzontles headquarters in San Pablo, California, including the talents of some of their academy�s students, the recording has real spontaneity to it. Arrangements are stretched by improvisations, sometimes by several different instruments on a single tune. The project also represents a great spirit of cooperation and diversity of language, culture, age, and gender. It includes the inputs of musical legends, seasoned pros, and amateurs. The wonderfully rich and often stereotyped musical cultures of both Mexico and Hawaii are represented here with the authenticity of lived experience.
Adios Ke Aloha: Waves of the Same Sea
is a worthy addition to Los Cenzontles� important work. Quoting Rodriguez again, �Culture is a fabric within which we are all woven.�

The musical partnership between Kalaniemi and Alakotila has thrived over a remarkable 35 years, long enough to the Finnish pair to develop a stunning intimacy and telepathy. Yet, what makes this music so fascinating in general, that is, beyond its unswerving ability to fill dance floors, is the fact that these two islands, part of the Paises Africanos de Lingua Oficial Portuguesa (PALOP) regions of the world, are the second smallest African country; Seychelles is smaller. There are only 12 villages on Sao Tom�, lots of rain forest and, not surprisingly, lots of rain. I mention this because one could be fooled into thinking, with music like what�s on offer here, there must have been a music scene larger than there actually was. Not that little was happening, but that less got recorded or released than it might have had there been a city such as Lagos or Nairobi with the studios, labels, and pressing plants to better document it all. The music here, like Volume 1- recorded during Africa�s so-called golden age- is known as Puxa, a complex stew of ingredients from other former African Portuguese colonies mixed with rhythms that, with the help of dancers, can summon spirits or exorcise demons. At least according to some. It�s worth knowing that a 100 years or so ago, the Portuguese banned Puxa dance; it�s also worth knowing they appear to have failed miserably at this silly endeavor. Tucked away in modern Puxa is merengue, Kompas, Soukouss, Benga, and much else. One suspects much of this is coincidental, while other grooves were definitely imported considering both Portuguese rule and the islands� location over the Atlantic from the Caribbean. But don�t be fooled into thinking these two islands don�t have their own thing, as the sounds on this collection show. L�VE L�VE Vol. 2: Sao Tom� & Principe Sounds 70s-80s - Pedro Lima Pedro Lima, who has featured in his own Bongo Joe collection, leads a fiery band, complete with choked guitar vamps tussling with a kit drummer as a lead guitar comments from the sidelines on �Sossegado.� Elsewhere, Sangazuza demonstrates what happens when the bass and keys drop out, leaving the drummers and guitars to ride out a groove and drive dancers mad in the process. Over 15 tracks, the collection shows off multiple guitars weaving and circling one another, with lead and harmony vocals constantly in response, becoming part of the songs� melodic framework. At any given moment, vocals give way as the music unspools and floats on grooves that must have gone on for hours live. Africa Negra�s �Apoi�mos a luta dos nossos irm�os� is one example. It captures the joy of post-1975 independence and only fizzled out as styles changed and musicians struggled to make ends meet. Yet, take a quick listen to recent RSTP programming, which features musicians such as Babilonia or Calema, and you�ll still hear Puxa rhythms, showing just how potent the music form this two-island nation is on a global level. items.body: Known for playing with County Joe McDonald, and for her experimental sound band The United States of America, Dorothy Moskowitz came back in 2023 with United States of Alchemy and their well-received release, Under an Endless Sky . In collaboration with avant-garde composer and filmmaker Francesco Paolo Paladino, and poet and music writer Luca Chino Ferrari, Songs of Compassion is eleven songs containing subversive and at times beautiful music, and richly evocative lyrics. Francesco Paolo Paladino and Luca Chino Ferrari | Photo by Maria Assunta Karini Songs of Compassion has two challenges for the listener. The first is the music, called variously avant-garde, ambient, modal, non-linear, and a few more. It is played mostly on pianos mixed in and out of the foreground, sometimes doubled, and sometimes out of phase, joined by strings, woodwinds, synth washes, and steely sounds. Initially disorienting, the music serves to remind us how locked our minds are to Western notions of harmonic movement. It speaks of alternative musical narratives much older and much further away. They are songs that subvert the song: more like Steve Reich than Steve Stills; more like Phillip Glass than Phil Collins. UNITED STATES OF ALCHEMY - Pale Wanderer At the same time, there are the poetic yet strikingly contemporary lyrics. �Pale Wanderer� talks about the fact that authoritarianism needs willing accomplices, describing what happens �When you make a deal with darkness.� UNITED STATES OF ALCHEMY (Dorothy Moskowitz, Francesco Paolo Paladino e Luka Chino Ferrari) by Silentes �Charlottesville� (written with the late Joe Byrd) evokes the time not long ago when torch-wielding nazis, proud of the metaphoric Ns on their tunics, chanted the antisemitic tropes paraphrased in Moskowitz�s words, �We�ll be one people, pure of race/No greedy throng could take our place� . Besides the overtly political lyrics, in the tradition of 1960s protest songs, there are also thoughtful meditations on mortality and our place in the universe. The message is high-minded yet sincere and direct. World weary and wise, Moskowitz�s voice inhabits the evocative philosophical lyrics with the authority of a skilled method actor. The melodies unfold like streams of consciousness, rising and falling, not following expected diatonic chord progressions, but honouring, instead, the value of each word. Moskowitz�s piano acts as another voice and sometimes a kind of Greek chorus commenting on the proceedings. The surrounding music frames, creates pulses and dissonances, and shimmers. The return of Dorothy Moskowitz with her renamed project has arrived in a moment quite similar to the times that spawned its predecessor. Political division, unrest, and uncertainty always generate artistic reaction, and United States of Alchemy roared back to life with their epic 24-minute opening track �Under an Endless Sky� in 2023, serving perhaps as an �In-A-Gadda-Da-Vida� for our times. Songs of Compassion continues to challenge how we think about our world. It�s music that defies the song form, while doing exactly what music is supposed to do�enrich the human condition. items.body: Those of us who have been digging into Analog Africa�s increasingly formidable releases over the last two decades are well aware of the massive amount of raw, vodun-based Sato and Sakpata-derived funk the label has issued by Benin�s most prolific 1970s-era band, the Orchestre Poly-Ritmo. AA has dropped no fewer than 3 compilations of their heaviest material, as well as a reissue of the band�s first LP, in an effort to give them the international status they deserve. That being said, what might be different about this collection of their music? And who is Antoine Dougb�? Antoine Dougb� et L'Orchestre Poly-Rythmo De Cotonou 1977 - 1982 (Analog Africa No.44) by Analog Africa As it turns out, Dougb� was a song-conjurer whose mode of musical transfer was slapping his legs in a rhythm known as Cavacha, a groove created by drummer Belobi Meridjo, who was inspired by a train cadence that he worked into a pattern that ultimately spread like a 21st century California wildfire throughout Congolese pop music in the mid-1970s. Dougb�, known as the �Devil�s Prime Minister,� was also a practitioner of vodun who inspired fear in any musician he felt was unsuited to play his music, which is how he landed on working exclusively Poly-Ritmo, as he felt they could nail what he wanted in ways other bands couldn�t. His recording career was brief - 3 albums and a few singles - but as this collection shows, it was potent. Antoine Dougb� et L'Orchestre Poly-Rythmo De Cotonou 1977 - 1982 (Analog Africa No.44) by Analog Africa Because of the era from which this music dates, it�s not surprising that the recording and instrument tones have changed - the guitars have a plastic sheen and synthesizers appear- even if the music remains rooted in the 1970s. Perhaps the influence of the Cuban son is more apparent here than on other Poly-Ritmo collections, especially in the collection�s initial offerings. And yes, Congolese rumba, then shaking all of sub-Saharan Africa to its knees, is present too. �Ma Won Min Towe Leo� is one example. Opening with a bed of synthesizers, the shimmering guitars, tinny, seemingly squeezed dry by the 80s themselves, lock in over relentless high-hat-focused grooves. The guitars finally start firing in different directions midway through, before that synth weaves back in, forming a bed underneath it all. Antoine Dougb� et L'Orchestre Poly-Rythmo De Cotonou 1977 - 1982 (Analog Africa No.44) by Analog Africa �We Tayi Sin Assi Tche� is much more overtly Cuban. With its insistent cowbell, classic, nasal vocal call and response, and tight, repeated guitar figures, its debt to mid-twentieth century Afro-Cuban sons is transparent. Another track, �Djomido Ma Dougbe Tche� rides a groove reminiscent of 70�s-era Franco classic �Liberte.� The pulse is relentless, and the guitar solo repeats a tight repetition of a few notes, driving listeners to ecstasy all the while. However, none of this music is a mere copy of its influences; rather, like so much potent pop coming from the continent at the time, it is a swirl of major influences rendered by local rhythms and vocal phrasing to give it specific identity, in this case, to Benin. Dougb�s musical role on this collection is a bit murky. One of his three albums has a photo of him, fully mic�d behind a collection of hand drums, so perhaps he served as a percussionist/vocalist; this release never explains. He wasn�t a songwriter in the traditional sense. It seems he was more of an instigator and arranger, but his thumbprint was apparently heavy enough to warrant his name on the records he was involved with. Whatever the case, in his brief run as a recording artist, he and Poly-Ritmo produced a handful of driving, Cavacha-inspired grooves that can still wear holes in club floors. items.body: Tako Toki are like desert island musicians who, castaway without their instruments, were forced to construct their own. Lucky for us, they are as skilled in making instruments as they are in creating original songs with which to show off their handicrafts. Un Dimanche � Monaco is the band�s follow-up to their well-received debut, Hirsute Farfelus , with a similar mash of musical styles. Before discussing the music, we need to talk about their instrument closet. They really have built everything they play out of bric-a-brac, odds and ends, and rubbish. I�m not sure from listening which is which, but they call their instruments, in an incomplete list, tassofons, tilofons, and tubofones, clarinuts, didjerimou, and klarbass, and my favorite, kitchenofon. (I will refer to what I hear by the names of store-bought instruments that they sound like.) The most surprising thing for me was how accurate the instruments were to pitch and how good they sounded under the harsh scrutiny of modern recording microphones that have documented a rich, high-quality sound. UN DIMANCHE A MONACO - LP by Tako Toki They have also very effectively matched their choice of instruments with the style of music that inspires their compositions. Right off the top, �Yinitza� features a laughing clarinet singing a klezmer tune accompanied by bassoon for the bass, frantic two-time percussion, and the exuberant human yelps found on many klezmer recordings. As on this track, many tunes feature improvisations that show an impressive degree of musicianship. On the cumbia-inspired �Le Cuenta,� the characteristic flute carries the tune, augmented by a Spanish singing chorus, and remarkably rich-sounding Latin percussion. The title track surrounds us with afrobeat woodblocks, shakers, and rattles scattered around the mix. The melody is played on a marimba ornamented with bells and cymbals. Again, the lead player improvises over the tune and often against the beat with jazzy chops. The flute returns on the samba-inspired �Ambiguidade,� and on �Aksum� it traces a trance-like Middle Eastern tune reminiscent of a 60s TV spy-show theme. UN DIMANCHE A MONACO - LP by Tako Toki Full of fun and one of a kind, Un Dimanche � Monaco celebrates our universal love of rhythmic, melodic, and harmonic sounds and the varied, wonderful ways cultures have organized that love in what we call music. At the same time, playing on literal pieces of junk, Tako Tiko reminds us, as we contemplate many mall music shops filled with gleaming wood and brass instruments and countless unused guitars lying in closets, that musicians will always find a way to make music. Tiny Sun creates tiny songs that give off light and heat well out of proportion to their size. Composed, performed, and produced by Martina Sorbara, Jonathan Goldsmith, and Don Rooke, the record is vaguely Americana, with plucked guitars and ukuleles, chiming keyboards, and the lonesome slide of the guitar.
Vanishment
contains eighteen sparkling miniatures - that take a scant 34 minutes to negotiate - notable for their economy of arrangement and the subtle directness of the lyrics. The tracks glow with Martina�s clear, high, and sometimes fragile voice.
The songs are about loss: lost love, lost confidence, but sometimes about resignation to the enigmatic quirks of the world. The tone of wry fatalism mirrors the fact that this project is the work of many years of collaboration and email exchanges while the trio pursued their musical day jobs. Jonathan Goldsmith is an award-winning composer for television and film, Don Rooke fronts the Toronto roots band The Henrys, and Martina Sorbara is known for folk, electropop, and her band Dragonette.

The stoic and twangy �Don�t Fault the Stars for Falling� could have been a Dolly Parton tune.

items.body: In August 1819, tens of thousands of working men and women gathered in St. Peter�s Field in Manchester to hear the politician Henry Hunt speak. They were difficult times, many still out of work after the Napoleonic wars, rising prices and low wages � and always those at the bottom of the heap suffering. Hunt was a famed orator, a man on the side of the people, able to stir and inspire with his voice. Although the gathering was peaceful, the size of the crowd terrified the magistrates, who panicked and imagined an uprising. They sent in half-trained dragoons and the cavalry, who rode down, slashed and killed without compunction or compassion. In the end, 18 died and up to 700 were wounded. It was a stain on the nation, an outrage; prompting Percy Shelley, one of the poetic giants of the age, to write The Masque of Anarchy , with its famous lines: �Rise like Lions after slumber / in unvanquishable number / She your chains to earth like dew / Which in sleep had fallen on you / Ye are many - they are few.� Peterloo, as people called it, remains one of the seminal events in English working-class history, one that Sean Cooney of the Young 'Uns has revisited for this album of original songs, which is lavishly presented in a book with contemporary letters, political cartoons and illustrations to create a multimedia event. It�s ambitious, no doubt about that, and he�s selected some great talent to help � guitarist Sam Carter, the almost ubiquitous fiddler/singer Eliza Carthy, Ben Nicholls supplying background and texture on various instruments, and the Lancashire industrial ballad singer Jennifer Reid, who doubles as narrator. Peter's Field by Sean Cooney, Eliza Carthy, Sam Carter, Jennifer Reid For a small ensemble, they make a powerful noise. The songs capture the feel of the day; the anticipation and excitement at the summer gathering, the joy that turns to terror and flight as the troops charge, then the bitter, mournful aftermath, voiced some powerful melodies and very well-chosen images. As a writer, Cooney often focuses on the personal in the small tales of people like �Sam Bamford� and �Mary Fildes,� while the three short pieces that comprise �The Monkey Rides The Mare� capture the bluster and arrogance of the soldiers. Peter's Field by Sean Cooney, Eliza Carthy, Sam Carter, Jennifer Reid Cooney is a persuasive singer, and on this heartfelt project, he puts plenty of emotion into his voice. Having two other outstanding vocalists alongside him makes for a wonderful triple threat. In these days when governments across the world are cracking down on protest, this stands as a sobering and very timely reminder. It�s a history lesson, yes, but the detail of the history stays in the book, while the music creates a set of songs that will resonate and remain for a long time. Find the artist online. items.body:
Live at Rockpalast 1999
documents a command performance at the Loreley open-air amphitheater by Malcolm �Mac� Rebennack Jr., aka Dr. John. Rockpalast is a live-music TV show broadcast since 1974 by Westdeutscher Rundfunk (WDR), the archival source for this CD-DVD package, and coincidentally a remarkable cultural institution on its own terms.
Taped at the height of Dr. John�s international popularity, backing the singer-pianist-guitarist are New Orleans stalwarts Bobby Broom (guitar), David Barard (bass), and Herman Ernest (drums), a tight quartet that projects authority and engages the crowd from start to close.
A striking UNESCO-designated World Heritage Site set, the Loreley is a slate pinnacle on a mythic horseshoe bend of the Rhine River, memorializing an enduring German literary legend both tragic and romantic. The setting is thus well-suited for Mac�s mystical spirit and lyrical style. By this stage of his career, he characterized his live show as a Mardi Gras revue with a mix of New Orleans standards and some of his most recognizable compositions.
Hence, he opens with the NOLA classic �Iko, Iko,� a half-sung, half-chanted celebration of community participation in the renowned Mardi Gras second-line street procession. Then comes the in-your-face boast �Qualified,� wherein the singer warns, �I got the power to control / I can see clean through you, blind mole / I want to tell you now, I'm qualified / You know that I'm qualified.�
Any Dr. John fan will recognize �I Walk on Guilded Splinters,� a moody, percussively insistent, foreboding expression of the Night Tripper�s immersion in �funknology� (his term), gris-gris herbology, and hoodoo incantation, punctuated with jungle growls and cries, a loopy, spooky slide whistle, and an extended psych-guitar solo: �Walk thru the fire / Fly thru the smoke / See my enemy / At the end of dey rope.�
Every piece in this well- honed set deserves considertion. Although Dr John lived for many years in Los Angeles and New York, his enduring hometown connection shows in the fond inclusion of his own �Sweet Home New Orleans� and �Goin� Back to New Orleans,� and he nods to a key influence with a funky rendering of Duke Ellington�s �I'm Gonna Go Fishin�.� Among other gems are Mac�s Top�10 hit �Right Place, Wrong Time,� and the instantly recognizable closer, Earl King�s �Big Chief,� another Mardi Gras burner.
Regarding his live performance approach, per the notes, �I always play a little bit of everything. I think that�s what music�s about: a little bit of somethin� old, somethin� in the middle, somethin� new, and somethin� as yet uncreated.�
Dr John's�s longtime fans will welcome this archival gem, which also is a solid introduction for any late comers to the party. Surmounting the barriers of language and culture, the power of
At the Rockpalast
is also evident in the enthusiastic audience response. As he declares, �If you�re gonna get off on somethin� you don�t need to know nothin� about it. Music is a universal language.�

items.body: Kr�ta , the latest release on Norway's Taragot label, features a Swede and two Norwegians playing interpretations of mainly traditional tunes from their respective countries. Fiddler Mats Ed�n has long been involved in Swedish folk music, as a player, composer and teacher, and in the process exploring and integrating different musical styles and approaches. Tellef Kvifte was in the pioneering Norwegian crossover band Slinkombas in the 1970s and has continued to play a central role in Norwegian folk music, both as a musician and an academic. Most often heard playing the sj�fl�yte , more widely known as a recorder, Kvifte has employed other instruments from outside the Norwegian tradition, in particular the saxophone and bagpipes. His son Knut Kvifte Nesheim , a drummer and composer, has also shown a determination to blur the lines between different musical genres, both in his solo and group projects. Kr�ta by Ed�n/Kvifte/Nesheim trio It comes as no surprise then to find this trio offering a far from conventional take on the tunes they have chosen. While dance tunes may be the source of most of the material here, this feels more akin to chamber music; not that it is remotely classical in style, but in the sense it conveys of three players engrossed in a musically intimate conversation. This is not a performance appropriate for accompanying dancers but might instead be seen as an exploration of hidden possibilities of meaning in the music. In so doing it reveals some of its underlying mystery, including, perhaps, a darker side. Just as in an Ibsen play, where the surface bonhomie, jollity and social nicety can be hiding something more sinister, in Scandinavian dance music there are at times hints of a troublesome undercurrent below the surface. So the decision to open proceedings with �Fossgrimen,� a fiddle tune from Norway's Setesdal valley, is perhaps significant. A fossgrimen is a mythical creature, a kind of water-sprite living in waterfalls from whom fiddle-players were considered to have learned their skills and for that were not universally welcomed, with the fiddle considered to be the devil's instrument. Kr�ta by Ed�n/Kvifte/Nesheim trio Tellef Kvifte takes the lead melody on most tracks but on the Swedish �Polska from Per Myhr,� having played a repeated introductory riff on the sj�fl�yte, with Mats Ed�n providing an amorphous textural accompaniment below and Nesheim adding some quiet tinkling, it's Ed�n who introduces the tune on the fiddle with Kvifte proceeding to play in unison. It's a short track and almost as soon as it gets going things start to fragment and everything grind to a halt.
